source.title: The Features at Convergence Theorem: a first-principles alternative to the Neural Feature Ansatz for how networks learn representations
source.authors: Enric Boix-Adserà; Neil Rohit Mallinar; James B. Simon; Mikhail Belkin

record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization on modular arithmetic using FACT-RFM, a kernel-based recursive feature machine rather than the small neural-network training setup in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports delayed generalization for FACT-RFM and NFA-RFM on modular addition. The tabular-data accuracy and sparse-parity phase-transition results do not report the delayed-generalization behavior specified by the claim. The modular-arithmetic feature-transform comparison is recorded separately; it does not test whether repeated neural-network runs converge to the same algorithm.
record.test_reason: The paper's subject is FACT, a weight-decay optimality relation offered as an alternative to the Neural Feature Ansatz. Grokking appears only as one benchmark showing that FACT-RFM, a kernel method, reproduces a known phenomenon 'similarly to the NFA'. The grokking evidence is a single figure caption reporting delayed generalization and 100% test accuracy. It gives no training-accuracy trajectory, no size of the delay and no data-fraction sweep. The system is a recursive feature machine, not a neural network of the kind the versions describe. NFA-RFM grokking is the cited result of Mallinar et al. [33], reproduced here as a comparator. So the study uses grokking as a target for its own method rather than testing whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but narrow. The authors' main conclusion is that FACT, derived from first-order optimality under weight decay, matches learned neural features at convergence better than the NFA and explains why the NFA usually holds. They also construct adversarial settings where the NFA fails but FACT holds. Their grokking point is only that FACT-RFM reproduces NFA-RFM's grokking and block-circulant features.
record.recipe_differences: The reported grokking result uses recursive feature machines with kernel-based fixed-point updates, not the neural-network training setup in the claim. FACT-RFM uses a FACT-based update; NFA-RFM is included for comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the unaveraged FACT-RFM update was unstable on modular arithmetic, especially in low-signal data regimes; geometric averaging improved performance and stability.

fits_no_version.finding: FACT-RFM (with geometric averaging) and NFA-RFM, both kernel machines, are said to show delayed generalization on (x+y) mod 61 with 50% training data, reaching 100% test accuracy within 75 iterations. The claim rests on a caption statement only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like delayed generalization on modular arithmetic also arises in non-neural recursive feature machines driven by AGOP- or FACT-based feature updates.

fits_no_version.finding: FACT-RFM and NFA-RFM learn distinct block-circulant feature transforms that both solve the same modular-addition split.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different feature transforms in recursive feature machines can solve the same modular-arithmetic task.

record.problems: The delayed-generalization result is reported for recursive feature machines rather than neural networks. The text does not give the training-accuracy trajectory, a numerical measure of delay, uncertainty, or results across training-set sizes for this experiment.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Tabular-dataset accuracy and sparse-parity results do not report the delayed-generalization behavior specified by the claim.
record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. Grokking here is a reproduction target for the authors' method, on a kernel system, with no quantitative evidence of the delay. The paper also reports that unaveraged FACT-RFM was unstable on modular arithmetic in low-signal regimes (App. E). That is a property of the method, not evidence about any version.

versions.untested_parts: The modular-arithmetic result uses RFM methods, not small neural networks. The text does not report training accuracy saturating while test accuracy remains at chance, or whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

rows.subject: FACT-RFM
rows.operation_detail: Trained FACT-RFM with geometric averaging on modular addition.
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe delayed generalization and report 100% test accuracy. The text does not give the training-accuracy trajectory or quantify the delay.
rows.check: The subject is the study's own kernel method (FACT-RFM), not a neural network. 'Delayed generalization' is asserted in the Fig. 5 caption only. No training-accuracy curve, delay length or chance-level baseline is given, so the jump described in V1 cannot be read.

rows.subject: NFA-RFM
rows.note: The authors state that both methods achieve 100% test accuracy and exhibit delayed generalization. The text does not give the training-accuracy trajectory or quantify the delay.
rows.check: This is a comparator kernel method (NFA-RFM) reproducing the cited result of Mallinar et al. [33], not a new test. The same issue as r1 applies: the delay is asserted in the caption without numbers.

rows.subject: FACT-RFM
rows.operation_detail: Compared the learned feature transform with that of NFA-RFM on the same train/test split.
rows.measure: Feature-transform structure and difference between methods
rows.value: Block-circulant feature transform; distinct from the NFA-RFM transform
rows.note: The paper says the methods learn distinct feature transforms while solving the same task.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The comparison is between two kernel update rules that the authors designed, not between repeated neural-network runs, so it does not bear on V6.
